messages.text: Mum, I'm looking at investing books for you
This one has a map of the world's stock markets
Japan must be a big part of it, right?

steps.prompt: All the world's listed companies together are worth a certain amount. What share of that is Japanese companies?
steps.reveal: About 5%. Japan is a big economy, but a small slice of the world market. Putting everything at home is betting on one slice. Simplified from real data.

steps.prompt: Imagine a bad year: Japan falls 40%, the rest of the world falls 10%. Change how much of Michiko's money is in Japan. Keep her total fall to 15% or less.

goal.hint: Japan is about 5% of the world. What if her mix looked more like the world?

steps.note: Illustration only. Real years can hit every country at once.

steps.title: Home is a choice, not a default
steps.body: Most people hold far more of their own country than its share of the world. That's [[home-bias]]. Spreading across countries is [[diversification]] on a bigger scale: when one market has a bad decade, it's only part of the picture.

steps.prompt: Why can spreading money across countries soften a bad year at home?
options: Different markets don't always fall at the same time or by the same amount
Foreign shares are guaranteed by their governments
steps.explanation: Countries move differently. Sometimes they all fall together, but rarely by the same amount, so a spread usually falls less than its worst part.

goal.hint: Leave the moves as they are and set the share in Japan to 15% or less.

messages.text: Mum, I'm looking for an investing book for you
This one has a map of all stock markets
Japan is a big part, right?

p1.prompt: Take all companies in the world that sell shares. How much of their value is Japanese companies? Guess.
p1.reveal: About 5%. Japan is big, but only a small part of the world market. Putting all money in Japan is a bet on one small part.

s1.prompt: A bad year: Japan goes down 40%, the rest of the world goes down 10%. How much of Michiko's money is in Japan? Change it so she loses 15% or less.
s1.note: Only an example. Sometimes all countries fall together.

t1.title: Your country is a choice
t1.body: Most people own much more of their own country than its part of the world. This is [[home-bias]]. Spreading money over many countries is [[diversification]]. If one country has a bad time, it's only a part of your money.

q1.prompt: Why can money in many countries make a bad year at home less bad?
options: Countries don't always go down at the same time or by the same amount
q1.explanation: Countries move in different ways. So money spread over many countries usually falls less than the worst country.
